list.listitem: Reye's syndrome is now an uncommon diagnosis; disorders that can present with similar clinical features (such as disorders of fatty acid oxidation or urea cycle defects) are now far more common. C
Transfer to a pediatric intensive care unit for monitoring and management. C
Management should address prevention of hypoglycemia, and treatment of cerebral edema and hyperammonemia. C
Testing to establish (or rule out) specific diagnoses, such as inborn errors of metabolism, should be undertaken. C

background.definition: Reye's syndrome is an acute, noninflammatory encephalopathy documented by (1) alteration in the level of consciousness and, if available, CSF containing 8 or fewer leukocytes/ul or histologic demonstration of cerebral edema without perivascular or meningeal inflammation; (2) hepatopathy (documented by liver biopsy or autopsy) that is diagnostic of Reye's syndrome or by a 3× or greater increase in the serum levels of AST, ALT, or ammonia; and (3) no more reasonable explanation for the cerebral and hepatic abnormalities.

list.listitem: Rare; the incidence peaked in the early/mid-1980s, and has declined sharply since then. The reason for this decrease may be related to the enhanced ability to diagnose disorders with a similar clinical presentation (such as defects of fatty acid oxidation), as well as the decrease in use of aspirin as an antipyretic agent in children.
The etiology of "Reye's syndrome" is uncertain; part of the definition includes the exclusion of other causes of hepatic encephalopathy.

It is often preceded by a viral illness (varicella, influenza, and others), and there has been a strong epidemiologic association with the ingestion of aspirin during that preceding illness and the subsequent development of Reye's syndrome in a patient.
The term "Reye-like syndrome" has been used by some authors to describe patients with hepatic encephalopathy who are found to have a specific inborn error of metabolism.

The pathophysiology of Reye's syndrome is not certain; it is speculated that either the viral infection alone or the viral infection plus a mitochondrial toxin disrupts mitochondrial pathways of beta oxidation of long chain fatty acids or of oxidative phosphorylation.
This can result in microvesicular steatosis in the liver as well as the accumulation of toxic metabolites. This, in turn, can result in liver dysfunction and cell death.
Hyperammonemia and hypoglycemia are common features of Reye's syndrome. Cerebral edema can be severe, and may be related to the mortality in Reye's syndrome.

Expanded newborn screening for disorders of fatty acid oxidation will detect patients with those disorders before symptoms occur; this will lead to better anticipatory management of patients with fatty acid oxidation defects and earlier recognition of metabolic crises in them. C
Aspirin avoidance in pediatric patients has been associated with a decreased incidence of Reye's syndrome, and avoidance of aspirin should be emphasized to parents of pediatric age group patients. C
A high index of suspicion is required. At this time, Reye's syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion. C
Reye's syndrome should be considered in patients who present with vomiting and altered mental status. C
Inborn errors of metabolism, particularly disorders of fatty acid oxidation or urea cycle disorders, should be excluded. These are more common than Reye's syndrome. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Characteristic abnormal plasma acylcarnitine profile and/or urine organic acid analysis
Characteristic abnormal plasma acylcarnitine profile and/or urine organic acid analysis
Characteristic plasma and urine quantitative amino acid analyses; urine orotic acid determination
History of known or possible toxin exposure
May have external evidence of trauma or history of headache prior to acute onset of symptoms

list.listitem: History of preceding viral illness (e.g., influenza, varicella, others).

History of salicylate ingestion during that illness (note: not all patients with "Reye's syndrome" have taken salicylates, and the possibility that other medications could also be involved has been raised but not proven).
Vomiting occurs 3 to 8 days after the initial viral illness.
Progressive mental status changes, beginning with lethargy, irritability and/or behavior changes and potentially progressing to coma.
The physical examination, other than the neurological examination, is frequently unremarkable.
Abnormal neurological findings can vary from lethargy and mild behavior changes to coma to decerebrate posturing to evidence of brain stem herniation.
Several staging schema for the neurological findings in Reye's syndrome have been developed (see ).

There is no single test that will "make" the diagnosis of Reye's syndrome: the following tests are useful both to help establish that diagnosis and to rule out other disorders that can present with "Reye's-like" symptoms if they are clinically suspected.
Arterial blood gas to rule out hypoxia and assess acid-base status.
UA (with particular attention to ketones) and serum glucose.
Tests of hepatocellular integrity (serum AST, ALT) and tests of hepatocellular function (serum bilirubin, blood ammonia, PT, and PTT).
Plasma quantitative amino acids, quantitative urine amino acids, blood (or plasma) acylcarnitine profile, and urine organic acid analysis to rule out metabolic disorders.

Lumbar puncture to rule out infectious or inflammatory causes of encephalopathy (if there are concerns about increased intracranial pressure, a head CT should be done to document no increased intracranial pressure before the lumber puncture is performed).
Urine toxicology screen.
Blood lactate (if there is metabolic acidosis).

Liver biopsy (for light microscopy and EM studies). Because of the ability to make the diagnosis using blood and urine tests of inborn errors of metabolism which can present in a manner similar to Reye's syndrome, liver biopsy for histologic studies may not be necessary as a "first line" diagnostic test.
Reye's syndrome should be suspected in a pediatric patient with mental status changes and vomiting.
Perform a careful neurological examination to assess state of consciousness and look for evidence of increased intracranial pressure.
As part of the initial evaluation, order serum glucose, AST, ALT, blood ammonia, blood gas, PT, and PTT.
Consider lumbar puncture, CT scan of head, plasma amino acids, plasma acylcarnitine profile, and urine organic acids if clinically indicated.
If Reye's syndrome is suspected, the patient should be transferred to a pediatric intensive care unit. C
Treatment should address prevention of hypoglycemia, treatment of hyperammonemia, and treatment (or prevention) of cerebral edema. C

Treat or prevent hypoglycemia: IV therapy with 10% dextrose in half-normal saline at full maintenance rate. Try to maintain blood glucose above 100 mg/dL. Be aware of potential for exacerbating increased cerebral edema.
Treat hyperammonemia: If a urea cycle defect is suspected, consider treatment with IV arginine and sodium benzoate/sodium phenylacetate ("Ammonul").
Manage coagulopathy (if present).
Treatment of hyperammonemia: if severe hyperammonemia is present, hemodialysis may be indicated.
If increased intracranial pressure is suspected, placement of an intracranial pressure monitoring device may be helpful to guide therapy.
Symptomatic patients in whom you suspect Reye's syndrome or related disorders should be hospitalized at a facility with pediatric intensive care capabilities.

Prognosis of Reye's syndrome depends on the severity of the clinical problems. Those patients with severe cerebral edema, elevated blood ammonia, or younger than 5 years had a higher mortality rate. C

Prognosis of inborn errors of metabolism presenting as a "Reye's-like" syndrome varies; anticipatory management, particularly during episodes of intercurrent illness, should lead to improved outcomes. C

Reye's syndrome is uncommon in pregnancy; other disorders such as acute fatty liver of pregnancy or disorders of fatty acid oxidation should be considered in pregnant women who present with a "Reye's-like" syndrome.

feature.caption: Stages of Reye's syndrome.
feature.feature_body:
Stage 1: Difficult to arouse, lethargic
Stage 2: Delirious, combative, with purposeful/semipurposeful motor responses
Stage 3: Unarousable; predominantly flexor motor responses; decorticate
Stage 4: Unarousable; predominantly extensor motor responses; decerebrate
Stage 5: Unarousable, with flaccid paralysis and areflexia; unresponsive pupils
Stage 6: (Unclassifiable due to use of paralytic pharmacologic agents)
From Belay ED, Bresee JS, Holman RC, et al. Reye's syndrome in the United States from 1981-1997. N Engl J Med 1999;(18):1377-1382.
